questions.question: Explain the purpose of VAT and how the output/input mechanism taxes only the value added, using the miller–bakery–shop chain.
questions.expected_answer: VAT is an indirect tax on consumption: businesses collect it but the final consumer bears it, and it is one of the largest contributors to national revenue, collected at every stage rather than one final point, which makes evasion harder. Each vendor charges output tax on its sales and reclaims input tax on its purchases, paying over only the difference. The miller sells flour at R100 plus VAT; the bakery sells bread at R160 plus VAT and, claiming back the tax on R100, remits tax on only the R60 it added; the shop does the same on its margin to R200. The businesses' payments together equal exactly the VAT on the final R200 the consumer paid.

questions.question: Distinguish standard-rated, zero-rated and exempt supplies with examples, and state the test that separates the last two.
questions.expected_answer: Standard-rated supplies carry VAT at the standard rate — most goods and services such as clothing, appliances and professional services. Zero-rated supplies are taxable at a rate of zero: staples such as brown bread, maize meal, rice, samp, dried beans, milk, eggs, fresh fruit and vegetables, vegetable oil and paraffin, protecting poor households, plus exports, which are taxed in the country of consumption. Exempt supplies fall outside the system entirely: interest-bearing financial services, residential rent, public road and rail transport and educational services. The test is input tax: zero-rated supplies are taxable, so the supplier still claims its input tax (often producing a refund); exempt supplies are outside the system, so no input tax may be claimed and the supplier absorbs it.

questions.question: Work the four VAT calculations at 15% and explain the treatment of bad debts, plus the ethics of VAT as trust money.
questions.expected_answer: Adding VAT: R2 000 excluding × 1,15 = R2 300 inclusive (VAT R300). Extracting VAT: R2 300 × 15/115 = R300. Finding the exclusive amount: R2 300 ÷ 1,15 = R2 000. Cost plus mark-up plus VAT: cost R1 200 marked up 50% on cost gives R1 800 excluding, then × 1,15 = R2 070 — mark-up first on the VAT-exclusive cost, then VAT on the marked-up price. The return is output tax less input tax, payable to SARS or refundable if inputs exceed outputs. Bad debts: on the invoice basis output tax was already paid over on a sale never received, so the VAT portion of the written-off debt is claimed back as input tax, and re-declared if the debtor later pays. Ethically, VAT is trust money — the state's money held by the vendor — so using it for wages or suppliers is spending what was never the business's, and frauds include private purchases claimed as inputs, fictitious invoices, and charging VAT while unregistered.
